paragraphs.source_en: Before answering, Kangetsu first gave a solemn cough, then deliberately delivered his observation in a calm, low voice: “Lately, girls, on their way home from school, or at concerts, charity events, and garden parties, are selling themselves, as if to say, ‘Won’t you buy me? Why, won’t you?’ So there is no longer any need to hire those failed vegetable sellers to cry out ‘Won’t you buy a girl?’ and conduct that vulgar sort of consignment sale. Once human beings develop more independence, this sort of thing naturally comes about. Old people, in their needless anxiety, make all sorts of comments about it, but to tell the truth, this is the trend of civilization, and I for one consider it a most welcome phenomenon and secretly offer my congratulations; as for the buyers, there are no longer any bumpkins who rap the head and ask whether the goods are sound, so that saves a great deal of trouble. Besides, in this complicated society, if one took that much trouble over everything, there would be no end to it. At that rate, even at fifty or sixty, no one would manage to find a husband or take a wife.” Kangetsu, being every inch a young man of the twentieth century, ardently set forth his thoroughly modern views, and as he spoke blew a puff of Shikishima cigarette smoke into Meitei’s face.

paragraphs.source_en: Meitei was not the sort of man to retreat before a mere puff of Shikishima smoke. He said, “Just as you say, today’s schoolgirls and young ladies are made, down to bone, flesh, and skin, out of pride and self-confidence; their refusal to yield to men in anything commands my deepest admiration. Take the pupils at the girls’ school near my place: they are quite something! They put on men’s narrow-sleeved clothes and hang from the horizontal bar. It is splendid! Every time I watch them doing gymnastics from my upstairs window, I am reminded of the women of ancient Greece.”
